This was what they did *in the days of Gibea*, perhaps the lowest point in Israel's history that Hosea, 400 years later, would compare to the depths Ephraim had reached ({{Hosea 9:9|Hosea 9:9}}; {{Hosea 10:9|10:9}}). 

- The path was cleared for a shift from charismatic leadership to "covenant-charismatic kingship." This kingship combined living under the Lord’s covenant with the anointing of the spirit for ruling, as seen with Saul and David.

The woman's father showed traditional Near Eastern hospitality, unlike the events that would later happen in Gibeah ({{Judges 19:14-28|Judges 19:14–28}}). The scene in Bethlehem offers reconciliation and the hope of a fresh start.
Some suggest the delay in leaving is like Samson’s seven-day bridal feast ({{Judges 14:10-20|Judges 14:10–20}}). However, it may simply show the father's reluctance to say goodbye to his daughter.
*Jebus*: See study note on Judges 1:21. The city kept its old name and foreign status in Israel until David captured it ({{2 Samuel 5:6-10|2 Samuel 5:6–10}}).

The two Benjamite towns, Gibeah and Ramah, hold an important place in Israelite history. They are linked with judges like: 

- Deborah ({{Judges 4:5|Judges 4:5}})

- Priests like Eleazar ({{Joshua 24:33|Joshua 24:33}})

- Prophets like Samuel ({{1 Samuel 8:4|1 Samuel 8:4}})

- Kings like Saul ({{1 Samuel 10:26|1 Samuel 10:26}})

Gibeah's noble history makes the tragic events that followed even more significant.

The usual hospitality rules in Israel and the Near East required a town citizen to offer shelter (compare {{Isaiah 58:7|Isaiah 58:7}}; {{Luke 14:13-14|Luke 14:13–14}}; {{Romans 12:13|Romans 12:13}}; {{1 Timothy 3:2|1 Timothy 3:2}}; {{1 Timothy 5:10|5:10}}; {{Hebrews 13:2|Hebrews 13:2}}; {{1 Peter 4:9|1 Peter 4:9}}). The Levite had money and supplies ({{Judges 19:19|Judges 19:19}}), so there was even less reason not to help. This lack of basic kindness shows the social problems during the time of Judges.
The old man came from the hill country of Ephraim, not from the territory of Benjamin. The people of Gibeah did not want to help.
*now I am going to the house of the LORD*: The Levite did not mention his status or explain why he was traveling.
The old man's urgent response hinted at the trouble to come (see {{Genesis 19:2-3|Genesis 19:2–3}}).
*wicked men*: Hebrew *sons of Belial;* see study notes on 1 Kings 21:10; 1 Samuel 1:16; 2 Corinthians 6:15. Their goal was to commit homosexual rape. Compare {{Genesis 19:4-5|Genesis 19:4–5}}.

*this man is a guest in my house*: It was shameful to be unkind to a visitor. However, the crowd's evil demands went beyond rudeness. They intended to harm the visitor (see {{Judges 20:5|Judges 20:5}}).

The old man tried to uphold the social duty of hospitality, even if it meant putting the vulnerable at risk (compare {{James 1:27|James 1:27}}). We cannot lessen the horror of what happened next, whether in their time or ours. The era of the judges was ending in extreme moral decay. Something was seriously wrong.
Compare the guidance given to husbands in {{Ephesians 5:25-28|Ephesians 5:25–28}}.
The Levite's actions show the terrible effects of a corrupt culture.

This Mizpah was not the one east of the Jordan linked to Jephthah ({{Judges 10:17|Judges 10:17}}; {{Judges 11:11|11:11}}, {{Judges 11:29|29}}, {{Judges 11:34|34}}). It was a place in central Israel. The name means “watchtower.”
The tribe of Benjamin likely got the message ({{Judges 19:29|Judges 19:29}}), so they knew trouble was coming.

- The "wicked men" ({{Judges 19:22|Judges 19:22}}) were important citizens (literally *lords*). 

- *They intended to kill me*: The Levite believed the men of Gibeah wanted to kill him after they killed his concubine.

The lots might have been the Urim and Thummim on the priest's breastplate ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}; compare {{Joshua 14:2|Joshua 14:2}}; {{1 Samuel 14:41|1 Samuel 14:41}}; {{Ezra 2:63|Ezra 2:63}}).

Israel acknowledged corporate responsibility. The leading citizens of Gibeah were guilty ({{Judges 20:5|Judges 20:5}}), and all of Gibeah became involved in their crimes by not disciplining them. The tribe of Benjamin had a responsibility to bring Gibeah to justice; by failing to do so, they all shared the guilt. If Israel had not addressed Benjamin’s wrongdoing, the guilt would have extended to the entire nation.

Benjamin's response matched its independent and warlike nature (compare {{Genesis 49:27|Genesis 49:27}}). The tribe had strong confidence in its famous warriors ({{Judges 3:12-30|Judges 3:12–30}}; {{1 Chronicles 12:2|1 Chronicles 12:2}}). Although outnumbered nearly three to one, they defeated the rest of Israel twice and caused many casualties ({{Judges 20:18-24|Judges 20:18–24}}).

- left-handeders: See study note on Judges 3:15. 

- The sling was like the one David used to kill Goliath ({{1 Samuel 17:40-51|1 Samuel 17:40–51}}). The slinger placed a stone in a small pouch attached to a leather strap. He swung it around his head to build speed, then released one end to launch the stone. A slinger could attack from a distance, unlike a swordsman.
To go first means to lead, but not always to come before ({{Genesis 49:10|Genesis 49:10}}).
The three battles occurred near the city. Despite having more troops and seeking guidance from the Lord, the Israelites were defeated by the defenders on the first day.
After a period of weeping and likely confession (see {{Joshua 7:1-26|Joshua 7}}), the Israelite troops received divine guidance and regained confidence.
A second disaster shook the Israelites' confidence ({{Judges 20:26-28|Judges 20:26–28}}).
The pressure to admit defeat and return home was growing. The Israelites intensified their activities in the Lord's presence, seeking his guidance.
On the third day, they used similar tricks and surprise attacks as when they took over Ai ({{Joshua 8:1-29|Joshua 8:1–29}}).
Baal-tamar is a town that has not been identified.
This section provides another description of the battle.

*overtook them in the vicinity of Gibeah on the east*: The geography is complex. There may be confusion between *Gibeah* and nearby *Geba* ({{1 Samuel 13:3-14:5|1 Samuel 13:3–14:5}}; see also {{1 Kings 15:22|1 Kings 15:22}}).

*the rock of Rimmon*: "Rimmon" was a personal name from the tribe of Benjamin ({{2 Samuel 4:2|2 Samuel 4:2}}). The place was about four miles east of Bethel. It was a stronghold, likely a cliff dwelling, that protected fugitives because it was hard to reach.
In Judges, for the second time, a foolish vow caused problems for those who made it (see study note on Judges 11:31).

The idea of a twelve-tribe league was important in Israel. It lasted despite Levi separating from the other tribes, Simeon and Asher almost disappearing, and Joseph splitting into two tribes (Manasseh and Ephraim). Losing one tribe would have implied that God's agreement with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob was falling apart.
Jabesh-gilead was an important town east of the Jordan River. Its failure to join the war against Benjamin caused a serious break in unity (see {{Judges 21:5|Judges 21:5}}).

- *The people grieved for Benjamin*: Israel worried about the nation's division. 

- The gap in Israel was God's doing, as the war against Benjamin was a response to God's covenant.
The yearly feast in Shiloh may have originally been a Canaanite celebration.
The land given to them was the land assigned to the tribe of Benjamin by the Lord's agreement ({{Judges 2:6|Judges 2:6}}).

The people of Israel persevered despite having no inspired leaders ({{Judges 17:1-18:31|Judges 17–18}}) and the tribal league's failure ({{Judges 19:1-21:25|Judges 19–21}}). Tribes and families remained strong, ensuring Israel and its tribes would endure.

The conclusion of {{Judges 17:1-21:25|Judges 17–21}} explains the reason for the social disorder of the time. After the period of the judges, God would establish a new covenant with Israel involving King David ({{2 Samuel 7:1-29|2 Samuel 7}}) and the promise of a messianic rule. The fulfillment of that promise would exceed anything imaginable during the time when Israel had no king.

5:17: The tribe of Gilad dwelled across the Jordan; the tribe of Dan cut across and crossed the Jordan and stationed their goods in ships; the tribe of Asher remained by the seashore, among the tired of the nation, they returned and built (fortified cities) and lived there.
5:18: But the tribe of Zevulun stood against the nations who blasphemed against Hashem — they gave their lives to death; and the tribe of Naftali — all the nations of the earth praise them.
5:19: The kings who were with Sisera came and fought; indeed, they fought — the kings of Canaan — in Ta’nach, they encamped and settled near the waters of Megiddo. They did not receive cash/silver spoils.
5:20: From Heaven they waged war with them; from the place where the stars go forth in their courses — there they fought with Sisera.
5:21: The Kishon River swept them away — that river in which miracles and mighty deeds had been done for Israel from earlier times. This was the Kishon River, there my soul trampled their slain warriors in strength.
5:22: Then the hooves of their horses were torn off, from the panic that came from before You, in front of of their charging warriors.
5:23: Curse Meroz! said Barak, the prophet of Hashem. Curse it and break its inhabitants, for they did not come to aid the people of Hashem when He waged war with the warriors.
5:24: Blessed above the blessing of noble women is Yael, the wife of Chever the Kenite — like one of the women who serve in the study halls shall she be blessed.
5:25: Sisera the wicked asked her for water but she gave him milk — to determine whether his thoughts toward her would be aroused — in a warrior's bowl she brought him rich cream.
5:26: Blessed is Yael, wife of Chever the Kenite, who fulfilled what is written in the Torah of Moshe: The ornaments of a man shall not be upon a woman, nor shall a man put on the ornaments of a woman. But she — with her left hand — stretched for the stake; and with her right hand for the hammer of smiths, to break the wicked and the oppressor. She struck Sisera, smashed his head, crushed his skull; she passed the stake through his temples.
5:27: Between her legs he sank, fell, lay; between her legs he sank, fell — where he sank, there he fell destroyed, Sisera.
5:28: Through the window Sisra's mother looked and gazed, through the lattice she said: Why is the chariot of my son Sisera’s delayed from coming? Why have the runners who bring me letters of victory been delayed?
5:29: Her wise attendants answered her, and she too responded wisely to tell them:
5:30: Do they not find and divide the spoils? They give to each man and to his household great spoils, before Sisera — spoils of embroidered garments dyed with colors on his neck, rich garments and precious vessels and precious items taken for warriors who plunder.
5:31: Like Sisra, so may all the enemies of Your people perish, Hashem. And the righteous who love Him shall be destined to shine like the radiance of His glory — one of three hundred and forty-three, like the sun emerging in its strength. And the land of Israel rested from war for forty years.
